title: How would you estimate how many hotel rooms there are in Paris?
description: A step-by-step estimate for "How many hotel rooms are there in Paris?" with the approach, the maths and a sanity check.
hook: The city of Paris has roughly 90,000 hotel rooms: about 37.5M guest nights a year, which is about 103,000 guests a night, sharing rooms at 1.5 per room, with rooms 75% full on average. You work backwards from demand to supply, and the key is getting occupancy and guests per room into the denominator the right way round. Have a go yourself before reading on.
body:
The question

How many hotel rooms are there in Paris?

"Paris" can mean two very different areas, so ask:

  • The city proper: the 20 arrondissements inside the ring road, home to about 2M people and most of the sights.
  • Greater Paris: the city plus the surrounding departments, including the airports and La Défense.

Also settle what counts as a hotel room. Short-term rentals and hostels are separate markets; mixing them in would blur the answer.

"I'll estimate hotel rooms in the city of Paris, excluding short-term rentals and hostels."

The approach: from guest nights back to rooms

You cannot count hotels from memory, but you can reason about visitors. Work from demand to supply:

  1. Guest nights a year = hotel stays × nights per stay.
  2. Guests on an average night = guest nights ÷ 365.
  3. Occupied rooms = guests ÷ guests per room.
  4. Total rooms = occupied rooms ÷ occupancy rate.

The last two steps are divisions, and candidates often multiply by mistake. Check the logic in words: if rooms are only 75% full on an average night, there must be more rooms than are occupied, so you divide by 0.75 to scale up.

Step by step

StepAssumptionResult
Hotel stays a year15M (tourists and business visitors, French and foreign)15M
Nights per stay2.537.5M guest nights
Guests a night÷ 365about 102,700
Occupied rooms÷ 1.5 guests per roomabout 68,500
Total rooms÷ 75% occupancyabout 91,300

Why these inputs? Paris is one of the world's most visited cities, so tens of millions of visitors a year is right, and 15M hotel stays in the city leaves room for day-trippers, people staying with friends and those using rentals. City breaks are short, so 2.5 nights is sensible. Couples share rooms while business travellers mostly stay alone, so 1.5 guests per room is a fair blend. Central hotels in a major city run fairly full; 75% is a reasonable average across the year.

Answer: about 90,000 hotel rooms.

Check against the real figures

The Paris tourist office's key figures for 2024 count 1,757 hotels and 91,154 rooms in the city of Paris, with average occupancy of 75.9% (Paris je t'aime, Chiffres clés 2024). Greater Paris had about 132,000 rooms and 50.9M hotel nights in 2024, at 72.7% occupancy. Our estimate is very close for the city; it would be well short if the interviewer meant Greater Paris, which is why the scope question matters.

Sanity check from a second angle

From the supply side. Paris hotels are mostly small, often in converted buildings with 30 to 80 rooms, plus a few large ones. Assume about 1,800 hotels averaging 50 rooms: 1,800 × 50 = 90,000 rooms. The two routes agree. (The real average is about 52 rooms per hotel.)

The occupancy reversal. If occupancy were 85% rather than 75%, the same guests would fill about 80,600 rooms. Higher occupancy means fewer rooms are needed for the same demand, not more. If your answer goes the other way, you have multiplied where you should divide.

What a strong answer sounds like

"For the city of Paris, about 90,000 hotel rooms. I get there from 15 million hotel stays of 2.5 nights, so about 103,000 guests a night, 1.5 to a room and rooms 75% full. A supply-side check, roughly 1,800 small hotels at 50 rooms each, gives the same. If you meant Greater Paris, I'd expect something closer to 130,000."

A weak answer multiplies by the occupancy rate instead of dividing, ends up with about 51,000 rooms, and does not notice that this is fewer than the 68,500 rooms already occupied on an average night.

Common mistakes

  • Multiplying by occupancy. Divide. Occupied rooms are a subset of all rooms.
  • Treating guests as rooms. Divide by guests per room before scaling for occupancy.
  • Ignoring scope. City versus Greater Paris changes the answer by about 45%.
  • Mixing hotels and rentals. Short-term rentals take some visitors who would otherwise use hotels; keep them out or size them separately.

Practise it

1. If guests per room were 1.6 rather than 1.5, how many rooms?

Show the answer

102,740 guests ÷ 1.6 = 64,200 occupied rooms ÷ 0.75 = about 85,600 rooms. More sharing means fewer rooms.

2. A major event brings 20% more guests a night, with no new rooms. What occupancy does that imply?

Show the answer

Occupied rooms: 68,500 × 1.2 = 82,200. ÷ 91,300 rooms = about 90% occupancy. That is close to full once you allow for rooms out of service and changeovers, which is why prices spike during big events.

3. At an average price of $250 a night, what is the room revenue of Paris hotels a year?

Show the answer

Occupied room nights: 68,500 × 365 = about 25M. × $250 = about $6.25B a year in room revenue, before food, drink and other services.
